courses.title: Online Media Management
courses.target_students: Section 1 for *BCOMM GDA, *BCOMM IMP, *BASC ARTS & TECH Year 3 & Year 4 students, Section 11 for TSM CRIM students only
courses.description: This course is designed for students to learn and acquire the knowledge of narrative strategies and cultural economics in relation with worldwide creative media industry. This subject will introduce the basic understanding of the online business models and the foundation of communication design entities and to the management concepts, which are specific to the process of communication design. Students will be able to identify and apply media economy to creative endeavors. They will develop an understanding of creative people as resources and individual talents in different commercial sectors and learn the strategic skills of project management and problem solving. In class, students will need to learn and understand the genuine practices of creative industry. Study of departmental works and role-play of operating a mobile and web creative company will be introduced. Students will eventually understand the business strategies and opportunities in the real world and what is necessary for a better creative media management.

courses.title: Virtual World: Design and Interaction
courses.target_students: For *BCOMM GDA and *BCOMM IMP Year 3 & 4 students
courses.description: This course aims to equip students with the fundamental principles and techniques to design and create virtual world environments which are suitable for virtual and augmented reality, games, and storytelling applications. Virtual world is a self-contained, persistence computer simulated environment in which player can inhibit, navigate and interact with non-player characters, and even communicate with other players in the case of multi-users shared and networked environment. On the theoretical side, student will first acquire a comprehensive overview of the historical development of virtual worlds from the early days of text-based virtual world to the contemporary graphic-intensive real-time interaction virtual environment. Besides, student will be introduced to the design principles and theories related to the different aspects of player’s cognition and perception of the virtual environmental. On the practical side, student will learn the essential techniques and skills to create an engaging and dynamic virtual environment with physical simulations, intelligent responses and real-time interactions. After finishing this course, student will be able to design and formulate a basic virtual world framework from which creative works such as virtual reality, augmented reality and games can be further developed.

courses.target_students: Section 1 for *BCOMM GDA, *BCOMM IMP, *BASC ARTS & TECH, TSM ITMP Year 3 & 4 students, section 11 for TSM CRIM students only
courses.description: This course provides a further study and understanding of digital design principles and visual practices through the narrative process. The learning goal will focus on the aesthetics as well as cognitive theory and applications of visual ideas and industrial standard by different creative media. The major learning activities will be hands-on practices in digital media and design experience of communication and transformation such as graphic arts, multimedia design and interactive content online. Exploration of content creations and media solutions in contemporary game and animation business are expected to be realized and delivered by students. Cross-media narrative skill and visualization techniques will be required to achieve the creative expression and idea. In addition, exploiting different visual skill sets together with demonstrations on professional techniques will be provided to students. After completing this course, students will be able to understand the discourse of design solutions and cultural changes in visual aesthetics and practices.

courses.title: Generative AI in Creative Practices
courses.target_students: For *BCOMM GDA Year 3 & 4 students
courses.description: Generative AI is one of the many types of Artificial Intelligence used to create various data, including images, videos, and 3D models. GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) is the most recent example, with ChatGPT creating original texts based on the existing data available on the Internet. Generative AI transforms how we communicate (transfer data) amongst ourselves and how we interact with computers, media, and digital technologies – and ultimately ourselves. It is already revolutionizing how we create digital media and, equally importantly, how we think, understand, feel, and know the world. This course will introduce students to the core concepts and fundamental knowledge of Generative AI – its present condition, history, and future possibilities. By using a transdisciplinary approach, a wide variety of theoretical perspectives and practices will be used to develop new knowledge of Generative AI. This course includes the application and use of Generative AI to enable computers to paint, write, compose music, and play video games. Students will learn the basic knowledge of deep learning and how it can be used to create images, text, music, and video games. More importantly, students will research why – how we came to this point, why humanity’s future is Generative AI, and the potential ethical, social, and practical issues of using Generative AI. While acquiring hands-on skills in using Generative AI tools to create different types of digital media, including games and animation, students will also learn to understand Generative AI and its applications in everyday life critically.

courses.title: Game Physics, Dynamics, and Simulations
courses.target_students: For *BCOMM GDA, *BCOMM IMP and *BASC ARTS & TECH Year 3 & 4 students.
courses.description: The course introduces students to different types of physics and simulations commonly seen in games and computer animations such as particle physics, rigid and soft bodies, collision detection, fluid and cloth simulations. Students will learn the underlying mathematical principles of these physics and simulations and also the effective implementations in game design. After finishing the course, student will be able to enrich their games and creative works to engage the audience with captivating real-time physics and simulations effects.

courses.title: Performance Animation
courses.target_students: For *BCOMM GDA and *BCOMM IMP Year 3 & 4 students
courses.description: The course focuses on body gestures in character animation for performance and storytelling. The course takes the animation from the level of a convincing physicality up to the level of an engaging performance with believable characters through studies and applications of animation principles, non-verbal communication, theories of human motivations and emotions. The course will provide a fresh perspective for studying character animation through technical and communication aspects of animation. Students will learn not only how to animate but also deliver the emotions and thoughts of characters to engage the audience with distinctive personalities and attitudes through rich and authentic body gestures.

courses.title: Creative Production in Extended Reality
courses.target_students: For *BCOMM GDA and *BCOMM IMP Year 3 & 4 students
courses.description: This course aims to empower students with the principles and techniques to harness the emerging interactive and display technologies to take advantage of the experience and knowledge learnt from the 3D digital content and virtual world creation paradigm to unleash the creative potentials of Extended Reality as an unprecedented storytelling medium. Extended Reality (XR) is a superset of all the technologies that includes Virtual Reality (VR), Augmented Reality (AR), Mixed Reality (MR), and anything within the spectrum of reality-virtuality continuum. Students will not only acquire a broad and comprehensive background of the histories, concepts, and principles of XR but also have solid practices down to specific realtime and cinematic VR/AR productions. Students will be able to apply the principles that transcend all forms of Extended Reality to inform the productions for burgeoning modalities of interacting with physical and virtual spaces. After finishing this course, students will be able to extend their knowledge and workflow from traditional 3D content creation to different forms of Extended Reality to develop creative works in ways never seen before.

courses.title: Implementation of Service-learning Engagement through Chinese Story Telling and Writing
courses.chinese_title: 服務學習與實踐：香港「老故事」書寫
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is a service-learning course. This course is an interdisciplinary course offered by Department of History and Language Centre. This course combines oral history skills with advanced Chinese narrative and reporting writing skills. It integrates theory and practice, such as key concepts and methodologies in oral history and ethnographic studies, strategy of narrative and investigation theory in Chinese storytelling and writing, interview preparation and reporting. As an interdisciplinary course, it would lead students to compare and contrast the two disciplines (history and literary) and integrate the methods and perspectives. The course also invites guest speakers such as social workers or professional trainers from NGOs, to teach students how to communicate with the elderly. Students will design and implement a Creative Community Service-learning Project to serve the elderly and society in Hong Kong or Mainland China. This course provides students with an opportunity to reach out to the elderly in the community. It aims to reinvent and innovate the tradition of storytelling and listening as students take down stories narrated by the older generation, preserving the culture and memories of a generation with words, and inheriting the wisdom and experiences passed down to them. Through these oral records, the students are able to understand the community identity of different groups of people and have a glimpse of the collective memories of generations before. This will enable them to have a better understanding of their community and learn from the life experiences of people from diverse backgrounds. The course will also cultivate the social awareness and sense of social responsibility of students by connecting them with people from all walks of life in their community. Students will write an individual online journals about their service-learning experiences in this course and reflect on how they connect between the service users, the trainers and social Others and the world around them. Finally, students will produce a Chinese booklet/multimedia output (e.g. a few pages of leaflet/a five minutes video), as a gift to those seniors, which record their personal history, collective memory and self-identity of the service users. The course ultimately improves the students’ ability to solve problems, communicate and work together as a team as they put into practice what they have learnt by serving the community.

courses.title: A Tale of Two Cities
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. This course provides a comparative analysis of Hong Kong and Singapore with regards to the development of healthcare system, housing, public transportation and education. In addition to their British colonial legacies, both Hong Kong and Singapore have experienced similar developmental trajectories: both competed as financial and commercial centres and served as hubs for multinational corporations. Students will learn the historical development of Hong Kong and Singapore. This course is designed to foster interdisciplinary discussion among sociology, politics and public administration in terms of theory and practice. Students will address how the Hong Kong and Singaporean governments deal with matters concerning healthcare, housing, public transportation and education empirically, comparatively and interpretively. Along with collecting editorials from various newspapers and performing social media data analysis, students are also required to complete simulation assignments where they act as decision-makers for various scenarios they may face in real-life situations. This course will equip students with critical thinking skills, decision-making capabilities in their own lives and leadership capabilities.

courses.title: Ecotourism in GBA (Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area): Planning and Design
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. The Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau Greater Bay Area (Greater Bay Area/GBA) is an integral part of the strategic planning of the country's developmental blueprint, which consists of trade and commerce, educational training, transportation and, perhaps most importantly, tourism. While it is important to enhance tourism exchanges and co-operation within the GBA, it is also necessary to pay attention to the importance of balancing economic growth and environmental (nature and culture) sustainability. The development of ecotourism is, therefore, a good option. This course explores a wide variety of issues related to the developmental blueprint in the GBA: economics, politics, human and community relations, and especially ecotourism. It will focus particularly on understanding the development of GBA through face-to-face field interviews with GBA residents. Students are expected to submit a group ecotourism planning proposal that includes analysis of tourism resources (Attractions), transportation arrangement and itinerary planning (Accessibility), infrastructure and facilities (Amenities), events management (Activities), and Accommodation. Students will present their draft proposals at the end of semester, before submitting the finalised proposals to the GBA-based organisations or local community. Through the experiential project students from different disciplines should learn how to explore related issues from different perspectives and how to solve problems by using multiple methods.

sections.instructor: Dr Ding, Jie (Academy of Chinese, History, Religion and Philosophy)

courses.title: Historic Landmarks, Heritage and Community
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is a service-learning course. Recently, keywords such as “user-friendly,” “popular-oriented,” and “public participation” have emerged as keywords in historical and cultural education. New approaches to history in the twenty-first century will involve more practical and experience-led teaching methods. Museums, cultural education centres, and historic landmarks will doubtlessly play an increasingly important role in stimulating public interest in historical education and heritage preservation. For example, the Jao Tsung-I Academy (饒宗頤文化館) which is located in Lai Chi Kok, is an extremely successful case of historic landmark preservation. Nowadays it serves as an important historical and cultural education centre in Hong Kong. This course is intended to provide students with an interdisciplinary approach and an in-depth understanding of the history and cultural functions of some important historic landmarks in Hong Kong. Special attention will be given to the study of historical and cultural relations between the landmarks and their neighbouring communities. In collaboration with NGOs and relevant community members, such as the Jao Tsung-I Academy, students will then form teams and undertake innovative community projects that explore opportunities for the landmarks’ continuing development. The discussion will encompass approaches from several academic disciplines, including History, Sociology, Geography, Marketing, and Business Management and Cultural Studies. The innovative community projects will then allow students to integrate academic content (theories) with community-engaged experiences (practices) throughout the whole process of service-learning.

courses.title: How Should the Government Spend Our Money
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. Should the HKSAR government spend more aggressively to improve the public livelihoods? What are the spending priorities? And whose money is it, after all? Students in this course will explore answers to these contentious questions in three stages—classroom classes for the basic knowledge, direct experience from community interviews and back-to-classroom reflection. Through this three-stage experiential learning, students acquire a deeper understanding of the subject of fiscal reserves. They come to realise that there is no simplistic black-and-white answers to the contentious questions on fiscal reserves. Rather they recognise alternative perspectives, contradictions and limitations. They also understand how demographic backgrounds, and economic and political circumstances may alter or invalidate their answers. The course prepares them to be more engaged Hong Kong citizens too.

sections.instructor: Miss Kwan, Janet W Y (Department of Accountancy, Economics and Finance)

courses.title: Taking a Stand: Turning Research Insights into Policy Recommendations
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. This course aims to help our students engage with public discourse on important social problems facing our local and global society. It introduces an interdisciplinary approach to analysing social problems, encouraging students to draw upon research insights and knowledge from different disciplines and share their insights with stakeholders such as the Hong Kong (HK) SAR government, NGOs and the public. Addressing a range of social issues facing Hong Kong and the wider global community, students learn to glean research insights from academic literature, to collect information from the HKSAR government under the Code on Access to Information and join the debate on such issues through experiential learning activities such as discussion with representatives from NGOs and/or community members and writing for the media. Working collaboratively in small groups, students will critically review the policies and decisions made by the HKSAR government and propose new solutions for social problems taking into account findings from their own research together with literature on the issues and/or policy ideas from other countries or cities. Students will eventually develop insightful and persuasive arguments on the issues and share their findings with the stakeholders including the HKSAR government and the public through a variety of channels, including writing letters to the editor and opinion pieces in the newspapers, submitting reports to the HKSAR government and engaging members of the community through online and offline activities. Moreover, the experiential learning provided by this course will facilitate meaningful connections between students and practitioners in the field to explore internship and/or employment opportunities.

sections.instructor: Dr Wang, Simon H (Language Centre)

courses.title: Design for Smart City: Towards a Sustainable Living
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is a service leadership education course. Cities and communities worldwide are facing complex challenges such as economic pressure, infectious disease, climate changes, ageing and healthcare, energy crisis, pollutions, resource shortage etc. By integrating emerging Information Technology, Business Strategy and User-centric Design, smart city solutions could enhance the liveability, workability and sustainability of our society. This course aims to develop a group of socially responsible graduates who have a vision of sustainable development and are able to apply technology to do strategic planning and design. Students will learn the concepts, framework and key technologies (e.g. IoT, AI, big data, cloud computing) related to smart cities and how they can be applied to different aspects of the society (e.g. transportation, healthcare, environment, accessibility). They will also learn how to research to understand and leverage related policies (e.g. Hong Kong Smart City Blueprint and the personal data privacy protection laws of different regions), and provide critical and ethical evaluation of the potential barriers and impacts for adopting the concept of smart cities from an interdisciplinary approach. In addition, students will also experience a hands-on training, for example embedded systems programming to help them create prototypes for smart cities solutions. Guided by the Design Thinking methodology, students will develop skills of human-centric design. They will work in groups to co-design feasible smart and sustainable solutions with community partners (NGOs, social enterprises, government offices, etc.) by applying key technologies learnt in this course and relating other knowledge learnt from their Major studies. Those smart solutions may contribute to accelerating one or more goals out of the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of United Nations (UN). In the co-design projects, students can deepen their understanding of sustainability issues and practices, and gain the opportunities to serve the community through field visits, guest lectures, public education or implementation of the designed solutions. Students may also apply entrepreneurship and marketing knowledge to develop service leadership plans or business plans, and promote their plans to be widely implemented in community services. For example, partnering with one NGO - an elderly care centre, students may take a leadership role to plan and project, first deepen the understanding of the current challenges of elderly care in Hong Kong by field trips or interviews with elderlies, and then lead the NGO staff and elderly participants to co-design smart healthcare solutions to monitor the elderly’s health status by applying big data, AI and IoT technologies. This solution may empower the NGO to provide better services to their beneficiaries with limited resources, while enabling the elderly to enjoy better quality of life. The proposal could be implemented in a small scale to prove the concept. The process of working with NGOs could enhance the digital capacity and bring digital transformation to the organisations This outcome may contribute to the UN SDG number 3: Good Health and Well-being. This group of students may also promote their idea to inspire younger students (e.g. a public demo) or turn their idea to a business practice. On completion of this course, students develop the sustainable development vision and leadership in strategic planning from aspects of technical, economical, ethical and policy. They may also get prepared to become a change maker and bring social impact to their workplace, community and the World.

courses.title: Bringing Chinese Culture into the Community through Art Activities
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is a service-learning course. The teaching and learning of Chinese culture is always a challenge faced by both local secondary school teachers and learners, yet being a language educator in secondary schools is one of the ideal graduate destinations amongst HKBU students. This course aims to offer our students a General Education capstone learning experience by exploring the essential facets of Chinese culture in the local context through engagement with senior high school working class students (F.4 to F.6), and bringing their interdisciplinary knowledge of Chinese culture as a rich source of cultural/literary/creative/artistic input to the community. This course will consist of five parts: (1) tackling contemporary issues and future problems in the learning of Chinese culture in Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Mainland secondary school contexts; (2) approaching Chinese culture by using exemplary Chinese texts and related reading materials from a perspective of cultural and literary critique; (3) designing teaching portfolios with the focus of one exemplary text or two based on the findings of the above parts I and II through the application of art activities (performing traditional ritual ceremony, making video clips, role-playing, travel log books, online interactive maps, creative writings, and so on); (4) providing direct service to local secondary schools; and (5) conducting a self-reflection session at the course Capstone Fair.

courses.title: Canine Service Partners for Inclusive Community
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is a service-learning course. The objective of this service-learning course is to maximise students’ exposure to experience taking an active role in co-creating values to the community with assistance dogs. They will explore the roles of assistance dogs in contributing to building an inclusive HK society from an interdisciplinary perspective through designing and implementing a service-learning outreach group project on assistance dogs. In the process, students will acquire the knowledge related to various aspects and issues about assistance dogs in work and community settings, appreciate the current research on the impacts of animal service on social well-being, learn the skills to develop events and/or activities to enhance the public and business sector’s awareness about the contribution of assistance dogs in an inclusive society, and be prepared to become ambassadors for promoting the work of assistance dogs. The course will facilitate personal development in which students will develop respect to assistance dogs and an open-mindset to create values for the community with assistance dogs. Special Note: This course is not suitable for students who are fearful of or allergic to dogs, and also those who are unwilling/unable to handle hygiene matters for dogs. Students may be required to attend an interview before confirming enrolment.

sections.instructor: Dr Cheung, Jamie Y H (Department of Management, Marketing and Information Systems); Ms TSO, Amy (Department of Management, Marketing and Information Systems)

courses.title: Data Storytelling for Gender Equality
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is a service-learning course. The aim of this course is to promote better use of gender data to inform policy making, enhance accountability and track progress towards the achievement of the Sustainable Development Goals adopted by all United Nations member states. More specifically, the course covers topics such as data visualization techniques, media messaging, statistical literacy, advocating with gender data and building effective communication strategies with data. This is an interdisciplinary course that involves gender studies, policy studies and communication. It aims to provide students with the relevant knowledge, skills and values that follow them to contribute to the advocacy and progress of gender equality for organisations, institutions and the society. The course has no pre-requisite and is open to any major. After completing this course, students should be able to (1) understand the impact of gender statistics in policy development; (2) integrate a gender perspective in collection, analysis and presentation of data; and (3) translate analytical results.

sections.instructor: Prof Luqiu, Rose L W (Department of Journalism)

courses.title: Fact-checking Misinformation and Disinformation
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. The rise of misinformation and disinformation has contributed to declining public trust in politicians and the media. This course will explore factors that make people vulnerable to misperceptions and conspiracy theories and why it is so difficult to combat the spread of fake news. The experiential learning course aims to enhance students’ media literacy skills and provide an opportunity for them to contribute to the public good by combating misinformation and disinformation.

sections.instructor: Staff 7 (JOUR) (Department of Journalism)

courses.title: Media Communication in the AI Era
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is a service-learning course. The purpose of the course is to arouse students’ awareness of the role media plays in their lives and the society in the age of AI and information. It aims at developing students’ critical and analytical ability to deconstruct media messages and information and giving students’ the opportunity to grow academically and civically through participation in a service-learning experience.

sections.instructor: Prof Lee, Alice Y L (Department of Journalism)

courses.title: Sport and Disability in the Hong Kong Chinese Media
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only; Section 00011 for *BA - SIM students only.
courses.description: This is a service leadership education course. In Hong Kong, people with disabilities make up about 7.4 per cent (499,400) of the overall population. ‘Sports for All’ is one of the key sports policies in Hong Kong to enhance and promote a physically active lifestyle in order to maintain good health. Sport can bring positivity to people and help reduce discrimination associated with disability(s) because it highlights the skills and the potential of the disabled and people from different age groups. This course is interdisciplinary by nature focusing on sports and health care, journalism, disabilities studies, management and serving learning. It will help develop graduates from different disciplines who can decipher the importance of leadership practised by sustainable leadership and situational leadership. The course will begin with introducing the definition of “Service Leadership”, the changing concepts of leadership regarding diversity, respect, discrimination and inclusivity. ‘Disability’ in historical and cultural context, sustainable leadership and situational leadership will be highlighted. Sports science will also be introduced. It continues with professional training of journalism, major reporting and filming skills and the analysis of the ecology of the social media. The distinct lack of “para-athletes”, namely, a sportsperson with a disability, in the mainstream media regarding both domestic and international participation at major sports events for para-athletes will also be explored and ethical issues considered by media executives, sports coaches, athletes and in disability sports reporting will be examined. The course will cover discourse (discursive analysis) in Chinese journalism because the social project is targeted at the Hong Kong public at large to address discrimination and raise awareness about the disabled and sports. As it aims at critically assessing the under-representation of para-sports and para-athletes in the mainstream local media, local news reports will be the major teaching resources used in lectures and most reports are in Chinese. The service project to be completed by students will include a series of qualitative in-depth interviews/conversations with local para-athletes from different sports such as archery, athletics, badminton, boccia, swimming, table tennis and tenpin bowling. The majority of the local para-athletes and their family members will communicate with students in Cantonese. It will lead students to dissect the social and cultural dimensions of the challenges that para-athletes are facing, and reflect on what role sports reporting can play in addressing the aforesaid issues and bringing potential changes. The in-depth communication with para-athletes will prepare students to be ready in embracing diversity, demonstrating respect and making changes to the working environment for employees or the service for those subjects who have disabilities.

sections.instructor: Mr Li, Hang Kei Matthew (Department of Journalism)
Mr Li, Hang Kei Matthew (Department of Journalism)

courses.title: Hong Kong Vision: Learning in the Village Community
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. This course is designed to be highly flexible in order to allow interdisciplinary discussion and critical analysis of the vision of Hong Kong’s future. Through exploring the political, culture, and social development of Hong Kong, students will be given the opportunity to share their perspectives on a wide range of issues and, perhaps most importantly, their vision for the future of Hong Kong. The issues and concerns associated with students’ vision of Hong Kong’s future may include rural-urban development, cultural diversity as well as environmental conservation and sustainability. Also, students are encouraged to embark on a community-based learning adventure, as they will be provided with multiple opportunities to encounter and engage with local NGOs and community members. This community-based learning project will help students become equipped with oral history skills and historical/anthropological knowledge.

sections.instructor: Dr Kwok, Kam Chau (Academy of Chinese, History, Religion and Philosophy)

courses.title: Taste, Environment and Technology: Food as a Lens
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. Food is not simply to fulfil the basic needs of human beings. Its production and consumption bear material and symbolic meanings in our everyday life. Through anthropological, sociological, political, and geographical lenses, this course examines three interrelated aspects of food: (1) taste (individual/collective patterns of choice and preference), (2) environment (natural surroundings, and socio-economic and political circumstances) and (3) technology (forms of production, processing, delivery and promotion). A special focus will be on Chinese societies. Students will learn the ways in which taste, environment and technology are constitutive of and influence each other. Contemporary social issues derived from food production and consumption such as food habits, health and lifestyle, differentiation and inequalities, affluence and poverty, waste and pollution, food security and sustainability, and localisation and globalisation will be discussed. To facilitate experiential learning, in addition to attending and participating in workshops and guest lectures, arrangements will be made to get students actively involved in community activities related to food issues organised by businesses, NGOs and social enterprises. Through participation in activities and engagement with various groups of stakeholders in the community, students will work as a team to apply the knowledge they have learned in the lectures and adopt an interdisciplinary approach to conduct a project to address an important food (food-related) issue at the local/regional/global level.

sections.instructor: Staff 6 (GSIS) (Academy of Geography, Sociology and International Studies)

courses.title: Financial Planning: a Pre-emptive Measure to Various Social Issues
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. This course is designed to help students realise the importance of personal financial planning to their future. Students will understand how to build a financial plan to achieve their life goals, both financial and non-financial. Other essential personal finance topics (e.g., budgeting, saving, investing, etc.) will be introduced to address financial problems in various contexts. To achieve the learning outcomes of the course, students will be required to design and deliver a financial planning or personal finance project for their chosen users (e.g., the youth, elderly, disabled, young professionals, unemployed, etc.). This experiential learning project will allow students to integrate academic content in solving real-world social issues.

sections.instructor: Staff 13 (AEF) (Department of Accountancy, Economics and Finance)

courses.title: Shape Our Future: Childhood Overweight and Obesity
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential Learning course. Obesity and overweight are considered to be health concerns across nations. Research suggested that children and youth who are obese and overweight are likely to stay obese and overweight into adulthood, and they are more likely to develop metabolic diseases as well as social and psychological problems. One in five students in Hong Kong is categorised as obese or overweight, and the data suggested a rising trend particularly in secondary school students. In this course, students will be guided to investigate the issue of childhood obesity and overweight in Hong Kong with the framework of Social Ecological Model (SEM) which is a comprehensive approach integrating multiple variables and layers that influence behaviour. Intrapersonal and interpersonal, community and organisational, institutional, environmental, and public policies factors are the layers included in this model. Students are expected to strengthen their knowledge in health science, nutrition, and behavioural science in the course and be able to explore various strategies to facilitate the weight management in Primary or Secondary school through an experiential learning activity. Students will work as a group to transfer the knowledge learnt from class and from other disciplines into practice by performing a comprehensive investigation based on the SEM that affecting the lifestyle of children in a selected school. At the end, students are required to prepare various strategies for the selected school to address the issue and to promote healthy living and weight management. Through the activity, students are expected to strengthen their knowledge, obtain new skills, and develop new attitude and ways of thinking towards the issue of childhood obesity and overweight, and recognise the challenges in weight management is more than just "eat less and move more".

sections.instructor: Prof ***, Rashmi-Supriya (Academy of Wellness and Human Development)

courses.title: Sports Performance and Health: The Marvel of Science, Technology, and Psychology
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. In addition to obtaining benefits of physical and mental health from doing exercises, large population would like to participate in sports competition in order to test their ability and as a motivation for engaging in regular exercises. Record breaking numbers of participants in Hong Kong Marathon every year and increasing numbers of community/school-based sports competitions proved the scope of participation. Therefore, scientific-based knowledge and skills in optimizing performance are essential as they can help with maximizing the physical function, performance in sports, and prevent injuries while injury is considered as one of the major drop out/suspension reasons in participating in regular exercises/physical activities. Besides, historical and cultural aspects will also be investigated in this course as they take important roles in affecting the evolution of sports and driving the advancement in improving the sports performance. This course will mainly focus on: (1) measurement and result interpretation of both health-related and sports-related physical fitness components; (2) the exercise and training prescription for performance improvement and injury prevention; (3) psychological and nutritional factors affecting sports performance. The theories and impacts of science, technology, and psychology on sport performance and testing will be emphasised and students will gain experiential learning by teaming up to work and apply the knowledge for improvement of performance for a group of participants in sports competitions with a holistic approach.

sections.instructor: Prof Pitsiladis, Yannis (Department of Biology)

courses.title: Service Leadership in Learning Communities
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is a service leadership education course. This course is intended for students of all academic disciplines. It is interdisciplinary by nature drawing on psychology, sociology and education. It aims to provide students with major theories of leadership (organisational psychology, sociology and business), service learning and learning community (education, management and sociology), and to equip them with the necessary skills to act as service leaders in supporting youth undertaking service learning activities in the community. The course will employ experiential and action learning approaches, which are rooted in the integration of concepts and theories from the above-mentioned disciplines, with a combination of in-class and out-of-class activities.

sections.instructor: Prof Sivan, Atara (Academy of Wellness and Human Development)

courses.title: Connecting the Elderly with the Internet - E-sports
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is a service-learning course. E-sports are often associated with youth, this course aims to break down barriers and promote engagement among young old (elderlies age >75). As many elderlies experience loneliness after leaving the workforce, E-sports offer a fun, interactive way to keep their minds sharp and reestablish social connections. Students will leverage their knowledge, skills and passion for gaming to introduce seniors to E-sports, fostering communication and camaraderie across generations. This service-learning course not only enhances the quality of life for the elderlies but also helps students develop valuable interpersonal skills. To celebrate the elderly's journey in learning new knowledge and skills, students will co-organise an E-sports tournament, showcasing their achievements and fostering team spirit. Redefine E-sports, elderlies, and team spirit! Let e-Sports be the bridge to a more connected, healthier lifestyle for everyone involved!

sections.instructor: Dr Chan, Wun Wa (Academy of Wellness and Human Development)
Dr Chan, Wun Wa (Academy of Wellness and Human Development)

courses.title: Art and the Community
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. This is a GE capstone course in which students address specific community problems, social issues and global discourse informed by knowledge and practice in community art, socially engaged art, inclusive design and other visual arts practice. Through a cycle of discovery, action and reflexivity, students seek to achieve the needs for the community and the public while develop deeper understanding and skills for themselves through experiential learning, such as identifying social problems through fieldwork, working with the community, seeking for social change through artistic and design practices, and through that to strengthen their interpersonal skills, leadership and citizenship. Engaging with professionals from diverse disciplines during the courses’ lectures, workshops/fieldworks will expose students to various data utilisation methods, enhancing their analytical skills and broadening their perspectives on possible policy development. The course requires students to engage in a community project in which through visual arts practice to create better awareness of a particular social issue and examine how to engage the public in that social issue through visual arts.

sections.instructor: Ms Fong, Wan Chi (Academy of Visual Arts)

courses.title: Empowering Citizens through Data: Participatory Policy Analysis for Hong Kong
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. In this course, the central focus is on enhancing students' understanding and application of data-informed public policymaking within the Hong Kong context. The objective is to equip students with the analytical tools and interdisciplinary approaches necessary to assess and influence policy decisions effectively. By integrating quantitative analysis with qualitative insights, the course aims to foster a comprehensive understanding of how data-driven strategies can be employed to address complex social issues, aligning with specific targets of the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Students will evaluate how much Hong Kong’s government uses data in policymaking, focusing on transparency, accountability, and effectiveness. Through practical projects and case studies, they will explore the impact of data-informed decisions in areas such as public transportation, health, and environmental management. A significant component of the course includes opportunities for students to request data from the Hong Kong government and engage directly with lawmakers (LegCo members) and district council members. This experiential learning approach enables students to gain firsthand insights and practical experience in the policymaking process. Ultimately, the course prepares students to become active agents of change in society. They will gain the competencies needed to navigate and influence the complex landscape of global sustainability challenges, equipped with the tools to implement and advocate for policy changes that contribute to the SDGs. This holistic approach not only enhances their analytical and expressive capabilities but also instills a commitment to lifelong learning and civic engagement in a globalised world.

sections.instructor: Dr Wang, Simon H (Language Centre); Dr Wu, Tian (Department of Mathematics)

courses.title: Connected Communities: Communication Technologies for Social Impact
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. This experiential learning course examines how communication technologies address social challenges that are aligned with UN Sustainable Development Goals. Students will explore the potential of digital tools to bridge divides, support mental health, and create inclusive environments through theoretical frameworks and hands-on engagement with local NGOs and tech organisations. The course critically evaluates technology-driven solutions' opportunities and ethical implications while equipping students with practical skills to design interventions that promote social good. Students will learn to assess digital initiatives and develop innovative approaches that leverage communication technologies for positive community impact through field visits, reflective exercises, and collaborative projects.

sections.instructor: Dr Serban, Florin Constantin (Department of Communication Studies)

courses.title: AI and Digital Inclusion in an Ageing Society
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. The application of AI-based and digital technologies has provided much convenience and alongside significant time and cost saving for average consumers and businesses. However, the widespread benefits of the technologies may not be enjoyed by everyone in the community, especially the elderly, Governments, international organisations and communities around the world have voiced concerns about AI and digital inclusion for the elderly. Understanding the characteristics of older adults, and their current and future digital device usage is vital for promoting digital inclusion. With a rapidly aging population, factors such as age, health, and socioeconomic background influence their engagement with technology. Recognising these issues, the World Economic Forum has indeed published a number of reports highlighting the importance on this agenda. Addressing these challenges is inherently interdisciplinary, necessitating the integration of knowledge from a variety of fields including technology (AI)/digital technologies, consumer behaviour, aging studies, social justice, and community development. Thus, the aim of this course is to furnish students with the chance to explore, through interdisciplinary lens, the effects of AI-based and digital technologies on the everyday experiences of the elderly. Students will explore the issues of population aging and digital inclusion in Hong Kong, as well as their relationship with the growth of AI-based technologies, robotic applications, and digital self-service technologies in daily life. The course will first introduce the facts of population aging in Hong Kong, the concern surrounding digital inclusion of the elderly, and the rising trend of robotic applications and digital self-service in business, with a focus on the retail and restaurant industries. It will then unfold the challenges faced by the elderly in adapting to these new technological applications in these industries from physiological, psychological, social and technological perspectives. Through a set of experiential learning activities, students will first identify the challenges faced by the elderly in learning and adapting to the use of AI-based technologies, robotic applications, and digital self-service technology, and then develop solutions to improve their experience in using these applications. For example, designing promotion and learning materials for guiding the elderly to use Chatbots, service robots, the digital self-service options in supermarkets and restaurants, or developing interactive tools for the elderly.

sections.instructor: Dr KATARIA, Pavandeep (Department of Management, Marketing and Information Systems)

courses.title: Partnerships for the Goals in Sustainability
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is an experiential learning course. The course is centered around the theme of ’Partnerships for the Goals’, with a speciﬁc focus on fostering collaboration among organisations towards achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It aims to empower students to be catalysts for positive change by exploring the interconnectedness between organisational operations and the SDGs, as well as among organisations. It particularly emphasises (1) diversity and inclusivity, i.e., social, and (2) biodiversity conservation and ecosystem diversity, i.e., environment. The course serves a twofold idea. First, it itself is a good demonstration of how organisations collaborate in producing sustainability ‐ based course content. Second, students will engage with various organisations, including (1) a theme park, (2) an animal welfare NGO / a service animal NGO, (3) a business organisation at the leading stage of the sustainability journey, (4) an accounting / consulting ﬁrm providing advice on sustainable practices, and (5) a professional alliance focusing on sustainable development. These interactions will provide students with practical insights on how organisations can partner to develop sustainability strategies and practices and, therefore, achieve sustainability goals. Speciﬁcally, students will engage in applied research through experiential group projects that require them to address speciﬁc sustainability ‐ organisation ‐ nexus issues provided by the above partnering organisations. These projects challenge students to leverage their knowledge and problem ‐ solving skills to analyse intricate sustainability challenges and develop innovative organisation ‐ level recommendations with a positive impact on both the organisations and nature and society. The course not only bridges the gap between theory and practice but also between diﬀerent academic disciplines, as it integrates principles and practices from various ﬁelds such as environmental science, business management, social sciences, and organisational behavior. By engaging with diverse organisations, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of how diﬀerent sectors contribute to sustainability. This approach ensures that students can draw on a wide range of perspectives and methodologies, fostering a holistic view of sustainability essential for addressing complex global challenges.

sections.instructor: Dr Ng, Brandon (Department of Management, Marketing and Information Systems)

courses.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Humanities: Exploring the Lives of Ethnic Minorities in Hong Kong
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is a service-learning course. This course examines the experiences and challenges of ethnic minorities (EMs) in Hong Kong, focusing on the South Asian community, which makes up 8.4% of the population. Since approximately 30% of South Asians aged 25-64 can only read and write in Chinese, these language barriers often limit their social mobility and opportunities. Moreover, over 80% of South Asians live with spouses of the same ethnicity, leading to further isolation from the Hong Kong society. This course emphasises emotional expression and communication through hands-on service learning. Students will engage directly with EMS, gaining valuable insights into their lives and perspectives. Harness cutting-edge AI tools to develop your communication skills and unleash your creativity by producing various art forms that foster meaningful dialogue between ethnic groups. The highlight of the course is a dynamic public exhibition where you’ll showcase your Al-generated artworks, amplifying the voices and stories of EMS in Hong Kong.

sections.instructor: Dr Chan, Wun Wa (Academy of Wellness and Human Development)
Dr Chan, Wun Wa (Academy of Wellness and Human Development)

courses.title: Transcending the Intergeneration Boundary:Applications of AI-Assistive Technologies for Elderly Care
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.
courses.description: This is a service-learning course. This service-learning course aims to enhance students’ understanding of the increasing demand for community-care services (CCS) catering to a rapidly aging population in Hong Kong and to enable them to explore the application of artificial intelligence (AI) technology for providing support for targeted elderly people in local communities through service-learning. Through collaboration with community partners and direct interaction with elderly individuals, students will develop and implement AI-assistive solutions to enhance social inclusion, well-being, and quality of life for older adults. Ethical considerations in the development of Al-assistive applications, the impact of technology on intergenerational relationships, and the unique needs of the elderly will be the key points of learning throughout the course. Students will work in groups to identify an everyday challenge facing each targeted elderly individual. These challenges can be physical, mental, or emotional and can impact the elderly's well-being on a weekly basis. Each group will be required (1) to conduct a literature review on the common issues facing elderly people, (2) conduct an in-depth interview to their targeted elderly individuals to identify their specific needs, and (3) to implement customised Al-assistive solutions to help improve the quality of life of the targeted elderly individuals.

sections.instructor: Dr Chan, Wun Wa (Academy of Wellness and Human Development)
Dr Chan, Wun Wa (Academy of Wellness and Human Development)

courses.title: Professional Investment Lab: Experiential Portfolio Management
courses.target_students: For Year 3 or above students only.

courses.title: China and the Contemporary Global Order
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.description: This course aims to (1) understand various changes in China through the lens of globalisation; (2) provide students with the evidence and skills to examine the global implications of China’s rise; and (3) equip students with the knowledge to interpret China’s changing roles in global affairs.

sections.instructor: Dr Yang, Shirley (Academy of Geography, Sociology and International Studies)

courses.title: Sustainable China: Environment and Development Issues
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.description: This course aims to introduce students to China’s environmental and development challenges in the context of ongoing social, economic, and political transformation. Students will engage with key theoretical debates in China studies, development studies and environmental studies to help them understand the complexities of China’s sustainable development. The course covers two sets of topics: (1) China’s socio-economic development and transition (China under Mao, economic reform, urbanisation, migration, inequality, poverty alleviation, rural development, and population policy); and (2) China’s environment challenges and solutions (air and soil pollution, water management, forest management, and energy and climate change).

sections.instructor: Dr Yang, Shirley (Academy of Geography, Sociology and International Studies)

courses.title: Global China Work Placement
courses.description: This course allows students experiencing globalisation in a working environment. It aims to (1) develop in students, a good understanding of the global-local interactions; (2) help students to integrate knowledge acquired form classroom learning with practical, everyday, working experiences; (3) enhance students’ awareness of transdisciplinary approaches to real-world problems and professional life; and (4) develop students’ soft skills such as communication, critical thinking, collaboration, creativity and empathy.

courses.title: Geography and the Contemporary World

courses.corequisite_text: Not for students already passed or currently enrolled in CHSG1005

courses.description: The course deals with the complex physical and cultural realities of the world. It adopts a topical approach, encompassing major issues in the contemporary world and studies these issues from a geographical perspective. It is designed in a manner that helps students to understand the varied and complex environmental interactions of the Earth. The course also assists students in recognizing the diverse ways in which geography can open new horizons and contribute to the building of an environmentally and culturally sustainable world.

courses.title: Cultures, Peoples and Landscapes
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.description: The course aims to develop students' understanding of the relationships between cultures, peoples, and landscapes. It does so by using a human geographical approach that recognises that politics, economics and power are key features of these relationships. On a more practical level it provides students with a valuable base for future and career development.

sections.instructor: Dr Lee, Ka Yin Anna (Academy of Geography, Sociology and International Studies)

courses.title: Earth Systems: Shaping Landscapes
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.description: This course is complementary with GEOG2016 Earth Systems: Atmosphere and Biosphere and introduces geomorphology and the main facets that have contributed to the study of landforms. Emphases are placed on: plate tectonic theory, as a framework to explain the major relief features of eastern Asia; on common geological materials and structures that control landscape in Hong Kong; and on the processes of weathering, erosion and deposition that produce contrasting landscapes.

courses.title: Introduction to Quantitative Methods in Geography
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.description: This course provides an introduction into statistical analysis of geographic data. Through real-world examples from various topic areas of geography, students learn sampling methods, descriptive and inferential statistical techniques for analyzing geographic data. Topics include hypothesis testing, spatial statistics, statistical relationships between variables, and how to generate, summarize and present geographic data, etc. The course will help students develop a solid knowledge basis for studying more advanced methods of geographic analysis in future.

sections.instructor: Dr YU, Howard (Academy of Geography, Sociology and International Studies)
Dr YU, Howard (Academy of Geography, Sociology and International Studies)
Dr YU, Howard (Academy of Geography, Sociology and International Studies)

courses.title: Energy Problems and the Environment
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.description: The ways how we produce and consume energy have far-reaching impacts on our economy, environment and society. This course focuses on energy problems and issues, and it aims to provide students a broad knowledge of the energy world. This course is organized in four sections. The first section “Energy, Environment and Society” examines the three major dimensions of energy: economy, environment and society. The second session “Energy Basics” guides students to develop a critical awareness of the key concepts of energy and the principles of sustainable energy. We also examine various energy sources, from fossil fuels to nuclear power and to renewable energy, and evaluate their relative advantages and limitations. The third section “Energy Policies and Politics” provides a broad understanding of the energy policy making processes, and examples drawn from Hong Kong energy policies are used. The final section is “Sustainable Energy Applications and Case Studies”. It introduces some of the latest developments of sustainable energy applications. We will draw lessons from global experiences.

courses.title: Geography of Health and the Environment
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.description: Throughout history, humans have thrived, lived, and reproduced in a wide range of environmental conditions. Consequently, geographic variability has long been an important aspect of health studies. Today, with the ever-increasing pace and magnitude of human impacts on natural systems, there is a growing need to understand and quantify the implications of these changes for global health. In this course, students will learn the intricate connection between environmental change and human health outcomes across various dimensions. We will focus on the role that environmental changes, such as deforestation, land-use conversion, urbanisation, human migration, international commerce, and climate change, play in shaping contemporary health issues at different geographical scales. The student will also do some research on specific topics such as the links between infectious and other diseases and the environment, the impacts of food production on land cover changes, the impacts of climate change on human well-being, and discuss economic and policy approaches to address these issues.

courses.title: Urban Geography
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.description: We live in an urbanising world today. It is, then, imperative to have a basic understanding of this still growing urban phenomenon. The perspective of urban geography emphasises the production of spatial differences among cities of the world. What is the nature and scope of urban geography? When, where and why did cities arise? How has globalisation affected the growth of cities? Why are cities in the developing world growing faster than those in the developed world? How do we understand urban systems within and beyond a country? What are the major socio-economic and spatial features of cities? What are the differences among the developed world and the developing world? These are some of the key questions to be addressed in this course.

courses.description: This course provides experiential learning opportunities for students to apply their knowledge and skills to tackle complex real-life problems via developing and organising field studies. Students will identify environmental or social issues for their field studies, in which they can engage the communities to obtain first-hand materials and feedback for their investigating issues. Students will have the opportunities to apply their interdisciplinary knowledge for designing a field trip study to investigate/research these issues. Four objectives are: (1) to establish students’ foundation for designing interdisciplinary field studies based on social, historical and cultural (etc.) contexts for environmental and social issues; (2) to encourage students to determine social or environmental issues, engage in the communities and learn from first-hand practical experience by organising field studies; (3) to give students authentic field study organising tasks in a team, for developing their multidisciplinary skills to integrate knowledge from different sources in real complex situations (e.g. diverse opinions on a topic, different work styles, conflicting time schedules, lacking financial supports); and (4) to offer a safe environment for students to reflect on their individual personal growth through organising field activities, so that students can identify their strength and weaknesses in terms of their roles in the community.

courses.title: Remote Sensing and Image Interpretation
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.description: Remote sensing is defined as the science of acquiring information about material objects without being in touch with them. These measurements are possible because sensors or instruments are designed to measure the reflected light from earth objects. Each kind of earth material has its own spectral characteristics, which enable us to discern the objects from their intermixed background. This course introduces students the basic concepts and skills of remote sensing technology. The principle of remote sensing is introduced first, followed by a review of available remote sensing systems including airborne and space-borne platform and sensors. Techniques of image interpretation and computer processing of digital satellite images are also practised.

courses.description: The course aims to introduce students to the foundational knowledge and skills necessary for developing basic AI literacies, which include: (1) Technological knowledge through an introduction to key concepts and principles underlying Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its emerging developments; (2) Practical applications by exploring potential uses of AI in various domains and learning how to effectively integrate AI tools into students’ personal, academic, and professional lives; (3) Ethical awareness by discussing the risks, debates, and impacts of AI, fostering responsible usage of AI technologies; and (4) Understanding human uniqueness and agency by examining AI’s broader effects on human well-being, creativity, critical thinking, and the sense of agency when collaborating with AI for social good. By addressing these aspects, the course ensures students acquire essential transdisciplinary competence to utilise AI technologies productively and ethically in their studies, future careers, and daily life. The first part of the course focuses on (1) and (2): introducing students to technological knowledge and practical applications of AI tools. Interactive lectures and tutorials will help students grasp fundamental AI concepts and complete basic lab exercises using AI tools. A flipped classroom approach will be adopted, providing students with video lectures and online materials to accommodate diverse learning paces and encourage active participation. The second part of the course addresses (3) and (4): fostering ethical awareness and understanding human uniqueness. Through lectures, debates, and scenario analyses, students will critically explore AI’s productive uses while reflecting on its impacts on human futures and responsible collaboration with AI for social good.

courses.title: The Rise of China: Historical Institutions and Modern Global Governance
courses.prerequisite_text: Not for students already passed or taking GFHC1036
courses.corequisite_text: Not for students already passed or taking GFHC1036
courses.description: This course studies how political, economic and ideological factors have affected the rise, the fall and the resurgence of China in historical and global context. After introducing the key achievements of China as an economic and trading power during the emergence of the ancient Silk Road, the course explores why China could not undergo an industrial revolution despite its early economic and technological leadership in the world. It then studies why Mao’s socialist transformation did not help China catch up with the West, even though the Communist victory in 1949 had ended China’s century of humiliation. The course then investigates how the reforms initiated by Deng after 1978 have evolved over time and brought China back to a major world power. The post-1978 development model is studied from the historical and global perspective, with emphasis on how major institutions have inherited from Mao’s time and changed gradually to their current forms. Students will be guided to contemplate the much-debated issues about the sustainability of China’s developmental model and the impacts of the Belt and Road Initiative. They are encouraged to form their own perspective with solid empirical reasoning founded on quantitative evidence.

courses.description: Do great leaders, thinkers, and artists determine the course of history? Or should we understand them instead as products of a particular time and place? In short: who shapes society? To answer these questions, this course turns to one of the most popular genres of historical writing: biography. We will study the works and actions of prominent figures in the arts, humanities, sciences, politics, and business in order to understand how people lived in the past and how societies have developed over time. Examining both the changes such people effected and the constraints they faced can offer insight into the balance between structure and agency as factors driving social change. By the end of the course, students will understand and appreciate different interpretations of the role of the individual in history, cultures and societies. This course will use the lives of carefully selected people from both the Western and non-Western world, including leading figures in students’ own majors, to develop a unique perspective on the history of various disciplines, professions, and institutions. We will look critically at some of the people who created the world we know today, consider how their reputations have changed over time, and reflect on the lessons we can take from their struggles and triumphs. Interactive learning activities in this course include group discussions and project presentations. At the end of the semester, students will submit a term paper examining the life and work of a prominent figure. As we pursue these projects, students will cultivate skills in research, analysis, and argumentation.

courses.title: An Introduction to Gender, Class and Race
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.prerequisite_text: Not for students already passed or taking GFHC1046
courses.corequisite_text: Not for students already passed or taking GFHC1046
courses.description: Gender, class, and race are three of the major categories that scholars in the humanities and social sciences use to structure their analyses. It is easy to see why: these categories represent important axes along which societies structure themselves and through which people develop a sense of identity. Broadly speaking, gender refers to social distinctions formed on the basis of sex; class refers to social distinctions formed on the basis of socioeconomic status; and race refers to social distinctions formed on the basis of factors such as culture, nationality, or physical characteristics. Yet while in popular discourse gender, class, and race can seem straightforward and self-explanatory, all three are social constructs—artificial frameworks that only appear natural when we use them unreflectively. None of them have stable, fixed definitions. This course focuses a critical lens on these three categories. We will ask: How do societies construct categories of identity like gender, class, and race? How have these constructions varied across cultures, civilisations and across time? And how do these categories intersect and shape one another? Examining the history of and relationships between these important categories of analysis will help prepare students to exercise responsible citizenship in a diverse, interconnected world. We will look at important theories scholars use to understand these categories and test those theories by applying them to real-life situations. Interactive learning activities for this course include group discussions, project presentations, in-class simulations and experiential learning exercises, and an enrichment activity.

courses.corequisite_text: Not for students already passed or taking GFHC1055
courses.description: The period between the early nineteenth century and present has witnessed the emergence of a “global” China that interacted and was integrated with the world on an unprecedented scale and depth. This course seeks to introduce undergraduate students to the global processes, practices, and communities that shaped modern China and the world, with much attention paid to their implications in the present day. It tries to explain the complexity of globalisation since the eighteenth century and its impact on modern China and, in turn, the ways in which China shaped the modern world. By engaging in discussion of seven interwoven themes, including communication, commodities, communities, food, practices, religion, knowledge, aesthetics, conflict, and the international order, this course aims to enhance students’ understanding of the interconnectivity of the world. It also highlights the importance of taking a transnational and transdisciplinary approach when studying history by expanding the students’ scope of enquiry beyond political or national histories.

courses.title: Building a Global Community: International Law and Politics since 1945
courses.academic_group: Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences
courses.prerequisite_text: Not for students already passed or taking GFHC1057
courses.corequisite_text: Not for students already passed or taking GFHC1057
courses.description: This course looks at the ties that bind people and societies across borders. Focusing on international law and institutions, we will consider whether and to what extent we live in a ‘global community’, and how we are connected to our fellow human beings. Combining historical and contemporary perspectives, we will consider whether we are getting closer to, or further away from, a true global community. The course comprises two broad strands. The first part introduces students to international law. What is it? How is it made? How is it enforced? The second part builds on those foundations by analysing key issues in contemporary world affairs, including human rights, war, and the global governance of trade and the environment. Taking specific cases, such as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Paris Agreement on climate change, we will examine the challenges of building a global community that is just, inclusive, and sustainable. Thus, the course introduces students to the human-made institutions, rules, and practices that comprise our global community. International law is particularly important, because it is a pillar of human civilisation and the source of so many of these institutions, rules, and practices. We cannot understand the societies that people have created, without understanding the laws that govern them. As this is an introductory course, no prior study of law is required. The course’s approach is transdisciplinary, drawing on history, political economy, law, politics, and international relations. Upon completion, students will have a deep understanding of how our global community works.

courses.description: This course aims to acquaint students with movement basics and practical ideas for doing physical exercises with small props and in a home setting. The home setting is a good starting point for building one’s confidence in physical ability as novice exercisers sometimes feel nervous or even intimated about going to a gym. One’s home can be an ideal place to practice conditioning exercises and get an exercise habit going. Daily home-based exercise is also an integral part to any rehabilitation program; elements such as joint proprioception, balance, and flexibility could be addressed by regular home-based conditioning exercises. Students will explore different body-weight exercises which bring about similar training effects as using typical fitness equipment or machines. In addition, students will be guided to explore toning and stretching moves using daily living items such as plastic water bottle, rope, books, towel, umbrella, and chair. Muscular strength and the ability to balance are vital to people of all ages if an active lifestyle is to be achieved. This course could potentially benefit the students as well as their family members as students would be asked to showcase what they have learned at home.
